about: Definitions of the technical terms on wcook04.github.io. The home page links the first use of each term in a block to its definition and shows it as a card on hover or focus. Edit here, then run scripts/build_hub.py.

terms.preview: A folder of written instructions, and optionally scripts, that an AI coding agent such as Claude Code or Codex loads when a task matches its description.
terms.detail: A skill's main file, SKILL.md, starts with a name and a one-line description; the agent reads the full instructions only when the task calls for them. 'Portable' means the folder works with any agent that reads this format. Narration IR is a skill of this kind: instructions for writing plans plus a small program that confirms each quoted passage is in its source file.

terms.preview: NVIDIA's open-source system that uses an AI model to turn English questions about a database into SQL queries and then runs them.
terms.detail: Auto Ontology imports a database and descriptions of its tables, then an agent built around a language model writes SQL for each English question, runs it and returns the rows. In Code Ontology Bridge it was loaded with a DuckDB database of its own Python source, through its own reader and import step plus a patch allowing other model providers.

terms.preview: A statement a formal proof assumes without proof; Lean can list every axiom a theorem depends on.
terms.detail: Lean's command #print axioms reports the axioms a theorem uses. Most Lean proofs rely only on three standard ones: propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. The Contextual Embeddings authors also state an axiom of their own, and General Reader shows which theorems depend on it.

terms.preview: A record of which functions call which, drawn as points for functions and arrows from each caller to each function it calls.
terms.detail: If function a contains the instruction b(), the call graph has an arrow from a (the caller) to b (the callee). Following arrows backwards from a function lists the code that could be affected if that function changed. A statically built call graph can miss calls made in unusual ways.

terms.preview: A function passed as a value to another function, which then runs it later, instead of being called directly by name.
terms.detail: In run_later(send_email), send_email is not called at that line; it is handed to run_later, which calls it afterwards. A call graph built only from direct calls misses this link. In the Code Ontology Bridge example, one of four functions in an answer was connected through a callback row, and without that row it was absent from the answer.

terms.preview: A program Claude Code runs at set moments, such as just before a command, which can let the command run, refuse it or ask a person to approve it.
terms.detail: Safety Core's checks run as Claude Code hooks. One hook reads each command before it runs; if a test or commit already failed in the session and the agent retries it with a setting the failed attempt lacked, the hook holds the command for a person's approval. With nobody to approve, the command does not run.

terms.preview: An AI model connected to a project so that it can read files, change code and run commands such as tests, usually in a loop until a task is done.
terms.detail: Claude Code (Anthropic) and Codex (OpenAI) are coding agents: each sends the model's chosen actions to the computer, such as editing a file or running pytest, and feeds the results back to the model. Both save each conversation, including commands and outputs, as a file on the user's computer.

terms.preview: A saved version of a project's files in git's history, with an author, a message and a link to the previous version.
terms.detail: Running git commit records the contents prepared in the git index as a new version. Each commit has an identifier, so any earlier version can be compared or restored. In the One Checkout and Safety Core videos, 'saving' a change means making a commit.

terms.preview: A Lean tool that checks a supplied proof against a separately written challenge statement, confirming the proof proves exactly that statement with only permitted axioms.
terms.detail: A challenge file contains the statement alone and a solution file contains the proof. Comparator compiles both and accepts only if the theorem in the solution matches the challenge statement exactly. For the Quartic Reader, Comparator accepted the main theorem and rejected five deliberately broken proofs.

terms.preview: Replacing a long conversation with a shorter written summary so an AI model can continue the work within its context limit.
terms.detail: A model reads only a fixed amount of text at once, its context window. When a conversation nears that limit, Codex's /compact and Claude Code's equivalent ask a model to write a summary that replaces the earlier messages. Agent Trace can copy a whole thread so that a summary is written in another chat, such as ChatGPT on the web, instead.

terms.preview: A programming language from Microsoft Research in which code carries written requirements that an automatic verifier proves before the code compiles.
terms.detail: A Dafny method states preconditions and postconditions; the verifier translates them into logic and asks the Z3 solver to prove them. Verified Dafny can be compiled to Python, C#, Java, Go or JavaScript. In Practical Formal Verification, deliberately broken copies of each proved computation are run through Dafny to show they are rejected.

terms.preview: A graph whose nodes are Lean definitions and theorems, with a line from A to B when A's statement or proof uses B.
terms.detail: In Quartic Reader and General Reader a program reads these lines from the compiled Lean, so they record actual use. The SK Reader's argument map is different: AI agents drew it from the papers and formal checks, and Lean does not check it.

terms.preview: A text description written at the top of a file, class or function in its source code, stored with the code rather than in a separate document.
terms.detail: In Python a docstring is a string literal placed first in a module, class or function, readable by programs at run time. Code Map reads descriptions that coding agents write in docstrings under fixed headings, such as a purpose line, so the map displays saved text and no AI writes anything new when the map opens.

terms.preview: An open-source SQL database that runs inside another program and stores a whole database in a single file, designed for fast analytical queries.
terms.detail: DuckDB needs no separate server: a Python program or command-line tool opens the database file directly. Code Ontology Bridge writes eight tables to a DuckDB file, including one row per function definition (code.symbols) and one row per call (code.calls), which Auto Ontology then reads.

terms.preview: One of the many questions posed by the mathematician Paul Erdős (1913–1996), now numbered and tracked as open or solved at erdosproblems.com.
terms.detail: Problem #257 asks: for every infinite set A of positive integers, is the sum over n in A of 1/(2ⁿ − 1) irrational? The terms are 1, 1/3, 1/7, 1/15, and so on. The general question is open; special cases, such as the sum over all n, are proved.

terms.preview: A research benchmark that adds many extra test inputs to the HumanEval programming problems, exposing faulty solutions that passed the original tests.
terms.detail: HumanEval is a set of 164 short Python problems with tests. The EvalPlus researchers generated additional inputs and found AI-written solutions (from ChatGPT, CodeGen and InCoder, among others) that pass the original tests but fail the new ones. Zenith uses those faulty solutions as bugs for a model's test inputs to catch.

terms.preview: The number a program returns when it finishes; 0 conventionally means success and any other number means failure.
terms.detail: Shells and tools such as git hooks read exit codes to decide what happens next. In a pipeline such as pytest | tail, the shell by default reports the exit code of the last program (tail), so exit code 0 can appear even when tests failed; the saved test counts show the actual result.

terms.preview: A paper that explains a result to any reader with general mathematical training, not only specialists, working through examples before the general proof.
terms.detail: An exposition assumes standard tools such as calculus, linear algebra and probability, but not the field's literature. It works small cases first so the main idea appears before the full argument. In the funnel it comes after the specialist paper and before the video; for Erdős problem #257 it is 16 pages. A specialist paper, by contrast, is written for experts in the field and skips what they already know.

terms.preview: The infinite sum of 1/(n³ sin²n) over positive whole numbers n; whether its running totals approach a finite number is an open question.
terms.detail: Convergence depends on how close n comes to a multiple of π, so it is tied to π's irrationality exponent. OpenAI's π paper states a consequence for this series, but its chosen Lean statement PiExponent covers only the exponent claim.

terms.preview: Matching a known transcript to its audio to find the exact start and end time of every word or phoneme.
terms.detail: Speech recognition has to guess the words; forced alignment already has them and only finds where each one occurs in the audio, usually with an acoustic model run over phonemes. The Montreal Forced Aligner and WhisperX's alignment step are common tools. It gives tighter word boundaries than the timestamps a recogniser produces as a by-product. The new videos' word times were taken from Whisper estimates, without forced alignment.

terms.preview: Google DeepMind's open GitHub repository of mathematical conjectures stated in Lean 4, each tagged with its status, such as research open or research solved.
terms.detail: The repository includes many Erdős problems. Its entry for Erdős problem #257 keeps the general question tagged open and lists Erdős's 1968 case as solved, with a link to the Lean proof in Will's repository.

terms.preview: Proving with machine-checked logic that a program or mathematical statement meets a precise written specification, instead of testing examples.
terms.detail: A formal proof is written in a language such as Lean or Dafny so that software can check every step from axioms and earlier results. The guarantee covers only the stated specification: a proof that a sorting function returns a sorted list says nothing about its running time or about code outside the proved function.

terms.preview: A program git runs automatically at a set step, such as before a commit, often to run tests or format checks and refuse the step if they fail.
terms.detail: A pre-commit hook in .git/hooks runs before each commit; if it exits with a non-zero code, git refuses the commit. One Checkout turns git hooks off for its commits, so the agents must run the project's required tests themselves.

terms.preview: Git's prepared copy of the files for the next commit, filled by git add and separate from the files on disk.
terms.detail: git add copies a file's current contents into the index; git commit then records the index, not the working tree. If one agent staged a file before another agent fixed it on disk, the staged copy still contains the old code, and a commit from it puts the old code back into history.

terms.preview: A text file listing exact line changes to files (lines removed and lines added, with surrounding lines for position), which git can apply to a version of the code.
terms.detail: A patch is produced by git diff and applied by git apply. Lines starting with '-' are removed and lines starting with '+' are added. One Checkout takes a patch the agent supplies, applies it to the last commit, and commits the result, without copying the whole shared file.

terms.preview: A git feature that gives one repository several working folders, each with its own checked-out branch, so agents can edit separate copies.
terms.detail: git worktree add creates another folder linked to the same history. Separate worktrees keep two agents' unfinished edits apart, but a fix made in one must be merged or copied into the other before that agent can test with it. One Checkout is for agents that already share one folder.

terms.preview: An arrangement of a system with the lowest possible energy; in Will's spin-glass films, the arrangement with the highest score.
terms.detail: On the four-arrow board in the sk-no-gap film, all 16 arrangements are scored and the best score is 7, reached by all arrows up and by all arrows down. With random Gaussian strengths, the ground state is almost surely unique apart from reversing every arrow.

terms.preview: Problems kept separate from anything the model or method saw during preparation, used only for the final measurement.
terms.detail: In the Zenith study the record of missed bugs came from 28 practice problems, and scores were measured on 58 other problems the model had not seen. The plan was saved with a timestamp before any held-out run, so the measurement could not be changed after seeing results.

terms.preview: A structured description that sits between a source form and a final output, so it can be read, edited and tested before the output is produced.
terms.detail: The term comes from compilers, which translate source code into an intermediate representation before generating machine code. In Narration IR the source is the spoken script and the output is animation code. For each sentence the plan records what it means, which sources support it, and picture changes attached to identifiers of spoken words, not to seconds. A person can read and correct the plan before any animation code exists.

terms.preview: A real number is irrational when it cannot be written as p/q with whole numbers p and q, q not zero.
terms.detail: Examples are √2 and π. A common route to proving a sum S irrational: assume S = p/q, so q·S is a whole number; then find a positive remainder smaller than 1/q, which is impossible for a fraction with denominator q.

terms.preview: The largest μ for which |x − p/q| < 1/q^μ has infinitely many fraction solutions p/q; it measures how well fractions approximate x.
terms.detail: Every irrational number has irrationality exponent at least 2, and almost every real number has exactly 2. Fractions such as 22/7 approximate π. OpenAI's paper in Plectis Atlas family 017 claims that the irrationality exponent of π is exactly 2, the smallest possible value.

terms.preview: A programming language and proof assistant whose small trusted kernel accepts a proof only after checking every logical step against the stated theorem.
terms.detail: In Lean 4 a theorem is written as a type and its proof as a term of that type; a file compiles only if the kernel accepts every proof in it. A Lean statement is the exact formal claim, so a correct proof can still prove something different from a paper's sentence. Mathlib supplies most of the background mathematics.

terms.preview: A proof written in the Lean language that Lean's kernel has accepted, meaning every step has been mechanically derived from the stated definitions and axioms.
terms.detail: Acceptance covers the proof of the formal statement as written in Lean. It does not cover whether that statement matches the problem in the paper (statement fidelity), and it says nothing about the prose papers or videos made from the proof. The quantum query result's Lean proof is about 29,000 lines. The reader websites link each section of a paper to the Lean declarations it describes.

terms.preview: A Python library for programmatic mathematical animation, created by Grant Sanderson for his 3Blue1Brown videos.
terms.detail: In Manim, each animation is Python code: objects such as equations, graphs and shapes are created, transformed and moved over time, then rendered to video. There are two main versions, ManimGL, Sanderson's own, and ManimCE, the community edition. The 3Blue1Brown style, pictures that change in time with the narration, is the model Will cites for the funnel's video level.

terms.preview: The community-maintained library of formalised mathematics for Lean 4, from basic algebra to analysis and probability.
terms.detail: Mathlib is developed on GitHub as leanprover-community/mathlib4 and reviewed by maintainers before each contribution is merged. Most Lean proofs of research mathematics, including the Erdős and quartic proofs here, import its definitions of real numbers, sums, limits and probability.

terms.preview: Model Context Protocol, an open standard by which an AI application connects to outside programs (MCP servers) that offer it tools and data.
terms.detail: An MCP server is a program that lists named tools, such as search_trace_threads, which an AI application like Claude Code or Codex can call and receive results from. Agent Trace's optional MCP server lets an agent search and read saved Codex and Claude Code conversations, the same records a person sees in its window.

terms.preview: A total Boolean function whose randomized query complexity is roughly the fourth power of its quantum query complexity, matching the known upper limit up to lower-order factors.
terms.detail: Since R(f) = O(Q(f)⁴) for every total function, the fourth power is the largest possible gap between randomized and quantum query counts. OpenAI's AI-written result constructs a function with R(f) = Q(f)^(4−o(1)), where o(1) shrinks to zero as the input grows. AI systems Will directs proved the result again in Lean 4, in about 29,000 lines.

terms.preview: A formal description of the kinds of things in a domain, their properties and the relationships between them, written so a program can use it.
terms.detail: In data systems an ontology names entity types (for example 'function' and 'call'), their attributes and how they relate (a call has a caller and a callee). NVIDIA's Auto Ontology builds such a description over database tables so that an AI model can map an English question onto the right tables, columns and joins.

terms.preview: A public registry of formal proof entries at palomar-registry.org, each recording a challenge statement, its proof files and the recorded checker results.
terms.detail: Will's Palomar entry for the Erdős work records selected results with challenge files containing the statements alone and solution files containing the Lean proofs. The saved result of 24 September 2026 lists eight theorems accepted by Lean's own checker and by a second checker, nanoda.

terms.preview: Programming Language Design and Implementation, the ACM SIGPLAN annual conference on programming languages.
terms.detail: The paper in General Reader, Contextual Embeddings: Implementing Bound Variables Through Instance Resolution, appeared at PLDI 2026 with its four authors' Lean proof released alongside it.

terms.preview: A diagram of a formal proof in which each node is a definition, lemma or theorem and each edge joins a result to a result its proof uses.
terms.detail: On the reader websites the graph is beside the paper. Scrolling the paper highlights the nodes for the section being read, and clicking a node opens its Lean code. The graph is built from the Lean files, so it shows the formal argument's actual structure rather than a hand-drawn summary.

terms.preview: The fewest queries a quantum algorithm needs to compute a function with probability at least 2/3, where one query may read a superposition of positions.
terms.detail: Written Q(f). Grover's algorithm finds a marked item among n with about √n queries, against about n classically. For total functions the gap between R(f) and Q(f) is at most a fourth power, and OpenAI showed functions that come within any smaller power of that limit.

terms.preview: The number of input bits an algorithm must read, in the worst case, to compute a function; running time is not counted.
terms.detail: The input is a string of bits hidden behind an oracle, and each query reveals one bit. For example, deciding whether n bits contain a 1 needs n queries for an ordinary deterministic algorithm. Deterministic, randomized and quantum query complexity, written D(f), R(f) and Q(f), count queries for the three kinds of algorithm.

terms.preview: The fewest queries a coin-flipping algorithm needs to compute a function correctly with probability at least 2/3 on every input.
terms.detail: Written R(f). R(f) ≤ D(f), since a deterministic algorithm is a special case. For total functions, Aaronson, Ben-David, Kothari, Rao and Tal (2020) proved D(f) = O(Q(f)⁴), so R(f) is at most a constant times Q(f)⁴. OpenAI's 2026 result gives total functions with R(f) ≥ Q(f)^(4 − o(1)), so the power four cannot be lowered.

terms.preview: An SQL query that repeats a step on its own results, used to follow chains such as caller of a caller of a function.
terms.detail: Written with WITH RECURSIVE, it starts from some rows and repeatedly joins the latest results back onto a table until no new rows appear. To find everything affected by changing function f, it starts at f, finds functions that call f, then functions that call those, and so on, often recording the number of steps from each one to f.

terms.preview: The first and longest written level of the funnel: the whole Lean proof written out in prose, step by step, meant to be complete rather than read end to end.
terms.detail: AI writes the record directly from the accepted Lean proof, so any section of the prose can be traced to the formal steps behind it. It can include routes that were tried and failed. For Erdős problem #257 the record is 152 pages. The shorter specialist paper and exposition are written from it.

terms.preview: A description of what each table and column in a database means, its keys and how tables join, in a form a query-writing program can import.
terms.detail: A semantic model adds meaning to a bare schema: for example, that code.calls.caller_id refers to code.symbols.id, and that a row in code.calls is one call from one function to another. Code Ontology Bridge writes these descriptions in Auto Ontology's import format, plus six optional saved queries such as one listing which function reaches which.

terms.preview: A spin-glass model of N up-or-down arrows where every pair interacts with an independent random Gaussian strength.
terms.detail: Each arrangement σ ∈ {+1, −1}ᴺ has energy H(σ) = −(1/√N) Σ_{i<j} g_ij σ_i σ_j, with g_ij independent standard Gaussians; Will's films use score = −energy. Introduced by David Sherrington and Scott Kirkpatrick in 1975. Reversing every arrow leaves the energy unchanged.

terms.preview: A short research paper written for experts in the result's field, which skips what the field's literature already establishes and spends its pages on the new steps.
terms.detail: In the funnel, AI compares the research record with published papers on the problem to sort standard steps from new ones, then writes in the form a paper in that literature would take. For Erdős problem #257 it is 26 pages, against 152 for the record. It differs from an exposition, which assumes general mathematical training rather than knowledge of the field.

terms.preview: A magnetic material or model in which pair interactions of mixed signs conflict, so no arrangement of the magnetic directions satisfies every pair.
terms.detail: Iron atoms scattered through copper are a physical example. In a triangle where two pairs favour agreeing and the third favours opposite directions, one preference always fails; this conflict is called frustration. Mathematicians study the low-energy arrangements of random models such as the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model.

terms.preview: Structured Query Language, the standard language for reading and changing data in relational databases made of tables with rows and columns.
terms.detail: An SQL query states which rows to return, for example SELECT name FROM symbols WHERE kind = 'function'. Queries can join tables on shared keys. Every answer in the Code Ontology Bridge study is a saved SQL query, so a person can rerun it against the same database and see the same rows.

terms.preview: Whether a formal statement in Lean says exactly what the informal mathematical statement says, with the same objects, quantifiers and hypotheses.
terms.detail: Lean can accept a correct proof of a wrongly formalised statement, for example one with a hypothesis that makes it trivially true. Statement fidelity is therefore judged by a person who reads both versions, or with tools that compare a proof's statement with a separately written one. Several of these repositories mark human review of statement fidelity as pending.

terms.preview: Examining a program's source code without running it, to record facts such as which functions exist and which call which.
terms.detail: A static analyser reads source text, usually by parsing it into a syntax tree, and reports what the text contains. Code Ontology Bridge parses Python files and records each function definition and each call it can resolve. Because nothing runs, calls built at run time (for example a function looked up by a string name) can be missed, and calls into Python's built-ins or outside libraries often have no identified target.

terms.preview: The program that runs code under test with chosen inputs, compares the outputs with expected ones and records each result.
terms.detail: Zenith's harness runs every proposed input on the reference solution and on each faulty version, applies the time limit, records whether each bug was caught, and can re-score stored model replies with no new model calls, so anyone can replay the scoring.

terms.preview: A value given to a program under test, chosen so that a faulty version and a correct version return different results or the faulty one crashes.
terms.detail: In Zenith the model sees only a description of a short program and proposes five inputs. Each input runs through the faulty code and a correct version; a different answer, a crash, or the faulty code running past a one-second limit counts as catching the bug. An empty list is the only input that catches one CodeGen bug.

terms.preview: Translating a question written in ordinary language into an SQL query that returns the answer from a database.
terms.detail: A text-to-SQL system receives a question such as 'which functions call parse_config?' and the database's schema, writes an SQL query, runs it and returns the rows. Accuracy is usually measured by comparing returned rows with an answer key. Code Ontology Bridge counted an answer correct only if its query returned the right rows on the real database and on eight altered copies.

terms.preview: Stopping a program that runs longer than a fixed limit; in Zenith, faulty code still running after one second counts as a caught bug.
terms.detail: The correct version of each Zenith problem answers almost immediately, so a faulty version that is still running after one second is treated as faulty. About half of the 69% to 77% rise came from larger inputs that made slow faulty code exceed this limit.

terms.preview: A yes-or-no function defined on every possible input string, with no promise restricting which inputs can occur.
terms.detail: A total Boolean function maps every string in {0,1}ⁿ to 0 or 1. Partial functions, defined only on promised inputs, allow exponential quantum speed-ups in query complexity; total functions allow at most a fourth-power gap between randomized and quantum query complexity.

terms.preview: OpenAI's open-source speech recognition model, which turns recorded speech into a transcript and can estimate a start and end time for each word.
terms.detail: Whisper is a transformer trained on about 680,000 hours of labelled audio. Word times can be estimated from its cross-attention weights by dynamic time warping (DTW), a method for lining up two sequences. WhisperX adds a separate forced-alignment step for more exact times. mlx-whisper runs Whisper on Apple silicon. Machine transcripts contain recognition errors, such as 'lien' for 'Lean'.

terms.preview: The start and end time of each spoken word in a recording, used to place a picture change at the moment a given word is said.
terms.detail: In a Narration IR plan a picture change is attached to a word, for example 'the turn finishes by the word down'. After recording, a speech recogniser such as Whisper supplies each word's start and end, and the change's time is computed from them. Times taken from a recogniser are estimates; forced alignment against the audio gives more exact boundaries. Re-recording changes the times, so events are rebound to the new words.

terms.preview: The project files as they currently are on disk, including edits that have not been staged or committed.
terms.detail: Git compares three places: the last commit, the git index and the working tree. When two agents share a folder, both edit the same working tree. One Checkout commits a patch without changing the working tree, so another agent's unfinished edits stay in the files it is using.
